_note: Narration script for the AO module 'Dementia and changed behaviours' (CPP-017-AO, CTL-094, CTL-011, CTL-122, CTL-123, with the PLST and NDB models from the SAAS CEP Semester 2 2026 Dementia session). Lee on eleven_v4, [calmly] prefix, two takes (scenes 1-4, then 5-8, 62.0 s and 64.1 s, both clean), take 2 raised 0.5 dB, joined with 0.6 s of silence. The prompt spelled PAINAD 'pain-add', EOC 'E O C', lorazepam 'lor-azz-uh-pam' and olanzapine 'oh-lan-zuh-peen'; captions use the text here.

lines.head: Joan, 84
sentences: Tonight, she doesn't know her husband.
She says there's a strange man in the house.
When he tried to help her, she pushed him away.
So, what is she trying to tell us?

lines.head: Behaviour is communication
sentences: Changed behaviour is rarely the real problem.
Most of the time, there's a trigger.
Or a need she can't put into words.

lines.head: Stress builds up
sentences: Dementia lowers a person's tolerance to stress.
And stress builds up through the day.
Bit by bit, she reaches the point where she just can't cope.

lines.head: Look for the cause first
sentences: So look for the cause first.
If she can't tell you about her pain, use the PAINAD score.
Watch her breathing, her voice, and her face.
And see whether she can be settled.

lines.head: Assess the risk
sentences: Dementia can make a person agitated, even aggressive.
Watch for the signs it's building.

lines.head: One calm voice
sentences: Don't argue, and don't correct her.
Acknowledge what she's feeling, and gently redirect.

lines.head: When it isn't enough
sentences: Care should be voluntary wherever you can.
Consider clinical support, and call the EOC Clinician.
They may recommend oral lorazepam, or olanzapine.
Then monitor her breathing, and her vital signs.

lines.head: Hand over what helped
sentences: Keep it calm in the ambulance, too.
And at handover, say what helped.
